 Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation

Nov. 1, 2026
Abstract

Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning–execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra’s success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks.

1 Introduction

“Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.” — Dwight D. Eisenhower

In physical manipulation, a failed attempt changes the scene, often irreversibly. Unlike simulated settings where an agent can call env.reset repeatedly on a target task to tune coordinate offsets, control scripts, or failure notes before evaluation [11, 20, 31, 49], a deployed robot must complete an unseen task within a single episode. Tuning procedures across repeated trials on a fixed scene also fits to that scene’s layout, and performance drops when object positions are randomized or the task changes. Generalization in manipulation therefore separates two problems: across tasks during development, using failures to improve the shared perception, control, and verification tools rather than task-specific scripts; and during execution on an unseen task, completing the task in one episode without prior trials, demonstrations, or resets (Sec. 2.1).

On a 210-episode diagnostic across all 42 tasks of the RoboDojo benchmark [4], the main bottleneck is physical execution rather than task reasoning (Secs. 2.2 and 2). When GPT-6 Astra is given a privileged action that moves objects along chosen waypoints without the robot arm, it succeeds in 76.2% of episodes; when it drives the arm through the benchmark’s reference end-effector interface (RoboProbe [60]), it succeeds in 22.5%. The model usually identifies the right object and destination, but the arm misses a grasp by a few millimeters, loses the object in flight, or hits a container rim during transport. Common control interfaces do not catch these errors in time. Step-wise and chunked action interfaces [37, 62, 60] issue motions from the latest frames without showing the full route in advance, so collisions appear only after the arm has moved. Program generation [21, 9] hands execution to a script that cannot see the scene, where normal program exit does not mean the intended contact succeeded.

We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that narrows this planning–execution gap within a single zero-shot episode (Figs. 1 and 2). In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions, while the harness measures the scene, checks and executes motions, and reports what happened:

  1. 1.

    Task-agnostic harness and explicit task belief (Sec. 3). Auriga contains no task-specific code, prompts, or heuristics, and exposes no privileged simulator state. One persistent model session plans the task, chooses actions, and recovers from errors. As an episode grows long, the model records its current plan, open questions, and task premises (pending, supported, contradicted, or unknown) in a concise task belief BtB_{t}, while full interaction logs stay in an off-context evidence record EtE_{t} retrieved on demand.

  2. 2.

    Preview and verification through a single admission gateway (Sec. 4). Every physical motion, whether called directly or from a model-written program, passes through the admission gateway 𝒜\mathcal{A} in a preview–execute–verify loop. While simulation is paused, 𝒜\mathcal{A} plans a multi-stage dual-arm sequence into a trajectory preview showing the path, step cost, and clearance warnings. During execution, the previewed trajectory runs while 𝒜\mathcal{A} checks model-set arrival tolerances τk=(δp,δθ)\tau_{k}=(\delta_{p},\delta_{\theta}), gripper openings, and observation checkpoints. If a stage misses its tolerance, 𝒜\mathcal{A} stops the robot and returns a receipt rtr_{t} with the completed stages, measured deviations, unexecuted stages, and fresh camera views so the model can recover from the current state (Fig. 2).

  3. 3.

    3D geometric measurements and finger-referenced actions (Sec. 5). On the input side, camera calibration, VGGT-Omega [46] depth, and SAM 3.1 [2] segmentation provide 3D object estimates, ray–plane intersection with height sensitivity, and two-view triangulation, together with in-hand slip measurements and warnings when a motion re-enters a past failure region. On the output side, the model sets goals at the finger contact region rather than the wrist, chooses tolerances per stage, and coordinates both arms on a shared timeline.

Auriga separates cross-task tool development from single-episode execution (Secs. 2.3 and 2.3). Over 13 development iterations (Fig. 3), manipulation failures were used to identify missing capabilities in 3D localization, contact checking, and state tracking, raising zero-shot performance across all 42 RoboDojo tasks from 36.2% SR (45.5 Score) at iteration #4 to 57.7% SR (64.0 Score) in the final harness. During evaluation, the harness is frozen and runs under the single-episode zero-shot protocol (Secs. 2.1, 6.1 and 6), with no target-task exploration, demonstrations, or resets:

  • •

    RoboDojo [4]. Across all 42 tasks and five dimensions (6,300 episodes over three seeds), Auriga with GPT-6 Astra reaches an average Score of 64.0 and SR of 57.7%, ranking first overall on the leaderboard across learned policies and agent methods, more than doubling the GPT-6 Astra reference harness (29.0 Score, 22.5% SR), and leading all 12 columns of the agent block (Tab. 4). On the 210-episode diagnostic set, Auriga closes 68.3% of the gap between reference arm control and arm-free object motion (Tab. 2).

  • •

    Scene randomization. Across the 12 Generalization tasks (Figs. 9 and 17), learned policies drop by up to 33.9% in SR on randomized layouts, whereas Auriga ranks first on both standard scenes (52.3% SR) and random scenes (45.6% SR) and achieves the highest generalization score (G=46.3G=46.3).

  • •

    RoboCasa365 [32]. On the 50 Target50 mobile manipulation tasks in unseen kitchens (250 episodes), Auriga reaches 73.2% Overall SR (92.2% Atomic-Seen, 67.5% Composite-Seen, 57.5% Composite-Unseen) without a learned policy or cross-episode memory, outperforming VLA-assisted agents RPent [61] (59.2%) and PyRUA-Lean [43] (56.4%) by 19.4% and 23.1% on composite tasks (Tab. 5).

2 Problem Setting and Positioning

We study zero-shot manipulation, in which a general-purpose model uses a shared robot harness to construct and execute a task procedure from the task specification and interaction feedback. We first define the single-episode zero-shot evaluation protocol (Sec. 2.1), then quantify the planning–execution gap that motivates our harness (Sec. 2.2), and finally position cross-task harness evolution relative to within-task trial search (Sec. 2.3).

2.1 Zero-Shot Single-Episode Protocol

Task and interaction.

The unit of evaluation is a case, defined by a task instruction and a specified scene variant, random seed, and layout. Each case starts from an initial scene and is evaluated under the benchmark’s execution budget and success criteria. The agent receives the task specification and accesses observations and robot actions through the shared harness. It uses the available observations and interaction history to choose subsequent tool calls or programs, then receives feedback from their execution. This interaction continues until success, termination, or budget exhaustion. The benchmark’s evaluator determines task success from the resulting execution.

Zero-shot protocol.

We define zero-shot evaluation through three conditions:

  1. 1.

    No target-task exploration or development before evaluation. Evaluation starts with a pretrained model, a fixed shared harness, and task-independent operating guidance. No preparatory exploration or trials are conducted on the target task, including its other layouts, to develop or select task-specific prompts, programs, skills, or policies. Model parameters remain fixed throughout evaluation.

  2. 2.

    No demonstrations at evaluation time. The agent receives the task specification and permitted observations, without additional solution examples or expert demonstrations. For memory tasks, the benchmark-defined event sequence forms part of the case’s observation input.

  3. 3.

    One execution per case. Each case is initialized and executed once, without a reset or rerun. Its outcome is recorded whether the episode succeeds or fails.

Within-episode adaptation.

An episode comprises successive model decisions, observations, and physical actions. During this interaction, the agent may inspect the scene, write and revise programs, preview motions, revisit its history, and recover from a failed grasp or placement. Recovery continues from the physical state left by earlier actions under the remaining execution budget, rather than resetting the scene to start over. Plans, generated code, and interaction memory evolve within the current episode and are not transferred to subsequent evaluation cases. Tab. 1 compares six aspects of target-task preparation and information available to the test agent across representative manipulation settings (scope and per-setting qualifications are detailed in App. A).

2.2 The Planning–Execution Gap

Deciding without the arm.

To separate what a vision-language model decides from how the robot arm executes it, we run the same harness with one additional privileged action, which moves an object along waypoints given by the model without using the arm. The model still chooses the object and every target pose from its own perception. The object moves under simulated physics, stops at a collision, and settles under gravity at the end, after which the action reports where the object came to rest. Success under this action therefore estimates what the model’s own decisions achieve when execution by the arm is taken out of the loop. We compare it with two executed systems on the same 210 episodes, five for each of the 42 RoboDojo tasks (Tab. 2). The first is RoboProbe [60], the reference harness released with the evaluation of GPT-6 Astra on RoboDojo [4], and the second is Auriga. Averaged over the five dimensions, the success rate is 76.2% with the privileged action, 22.5% for RoboProbe, and 59.2% for Auriga. The model therefore decides considerably better than it executes, and Auriga recovers 68.3% of this planning–execution gap in SR (70.6% in Score).

Why common paradigms leave the gap open.

Two common ways of placing a general model on a robot address execution only indirectly. In step-wise action output, as in the reference harness and in VLA policies [37, 62, 60], the model emits one motion step or chunk per call from the latest frames. It never sees the route of a motion before committing to it, and a failed motion is noticed only when the model reads the next frame, by which time the arm has already moved. In code as policy [21, 9], the model writes a program that commands the control interface directly. Execution judgment then moves into a program that cannot see the scene. A failure is detected only if the program was written to check for it, and a program may exit normally even after the motions it requested have failed. Auriga keeps the judgment with the model, which describes a complete action sequence in each call rather than a single step. Before execution, the model can see the whole trajectory, its cost, and its projection on the camera image (Sec. 4.1), and the harness checks the measured outcome after every movement (Sec. 4.2).

2.3 General-Purpose Harness Evolution

Improvement in embodied agents can target either a procedure for a particular task or the shared capabilities used across many tasks [8, 63].

Within-task trial search versus cross-task tool evolution.

Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI) groups autonomous improvement into six levels from L0 to L5 [8]:

  • •

    L0–L2 (within-task search and refinement): Under a single-task objective, the system repeats trials to adjust a trajectory, script, or task note, so the resulting gains stay mainly on the practiced task.

  • •

    L3–L4 (cross-task experience and tool evolution): The system turns recurring failures across different tasks into reusable tools, interfaces, and verification steps that apply to unseen tasks.

  • •

    L5 (meta-improvement): The system revises its own perception, control, and verification mechanisms so that later tasks are solved more reliably.

Target-task refinement methods such as HexaShell, EmbodiedEvo, and SEAR [11, 20, 49] work in the L0–L2 regime: they reset the target scene across trials to tune coordinate offsets, scripts, or failure notes for that task, which improves performance on the practiced layout but can overfit when layouts change. Auriga instead focuses on L3–L5 evolution during development. Failures such as a jammed pin insertion or a slipped cloth grasp are used not to add a coordinate offset for that scene, but to diagnose missing capabilities in 3D localization, contact checking, or in-hand state tracking and to upgrade the shared tools accordingly.

Role of the harness.

An agent harness connects the model to the robot: it translates the model’s intent into motion and stops the robot when contact or slippage occurs, without making task decisions on the model’s behalf. Existing harnesses often either run generated commands open-loop without checking the physical outcome, or add task-specific rules and thresholds in the backend to pass particular tasks. Because manipulation involves both tight rigid clearances and deformable objects, an offset or grasp rule tuned for one task often interferes with another. Auriga keeps the harness task-agnostic through three rules: (1) no task-specific logic or privileged state, so the same code and prompts run across all tasks and randomized layouts; (2) general measurement and control tools, including calibrated multi-view triangulation, paused-world trajectory preview, stage tolerances, and in-hand slip checks; and (3) in-place recovery, stopping when a motion leaves its tolerance and returning the measured deviation so the model can continue from the current state.

Two complementary timescales and capability trajectory.

System development and within-episode adaptation operate at complementary timescales. Across 13 development iterations (#0 to #12, Fig. 3), recurring execution bottlenecks across diverse tasks drove task-agnostic upgrades to the shared harness, lifting the RoboDojo Score from 21.5 (4.0% SR on the 50-case diagnostic set) at the initial base-model loop (#0) to 45.5 (36.2% SR across all 42 tasks) at #4 and 64.0 (57.7% SR across 6,300 episodes) at #12, with consistent gains across all five capability dimensions (+16.8+16.8 Score in Generalization, +5.6+5.6 in Precision, +29.5+29.5 in Long-Horizon, +30.8+30.8 in Memory, and +9.8+9.8 in Open; inset of Fig. 3). These 13 milestones organize into the three architectural pillars detailed in the next three sections:

  1. 1.

    Structured task belief and evidence records (Sec. 3): refactoring the harness around verbatim task specifications (#4, 45.5 Score), maintaining an explicit evidence ledger (#5), and adding structured history retrieval (#6, 46.6 Score);

  2. 2.

    Admission gateway with preview and stage verification (Sec. 4): previewing candidate trajectories while simulation is paused (#2, 26.2 Score), supporting in-place transport recovery (#8), and enforcing stage arrival tolerances and obstacle clearance checks (#9, 53.4 Score);

  3. 3.

    Calibrated 3D perception and expressive action interfaces (Sec. 5): unifying dual-arm timelines (#3, 30.0 Score), adding multi-view 3D triangulation (#6), ROI zoom (#7, 49.9 Score), held-object perception (#10), explicit motion control (#11, 58.8 Score), and VGGT-Omega / SAM 3.1 geometric perception (#12, 64.0 Score).

During evaluation, the harness version (#12) is completely frozen across all cases. Within each evaluated episode, the model uses these shared tools to inspect the scene, diagnose discrepancies, and revise its plan or generated programs from execution feedback, continuing from the physical state left by previous actions under the remaining budget without an environment reset or cross-episode memory transfer.

3 System Overview

Large vision-language models can reason about task structure, but reliable manipulation also requires metric scene information, contact-sensitive execution, and feedback after each action. Auriga addresses this gap with a simple closed-loop workflow: the model measures and previews while the simulation is paused, submits a physical action through a single admission gateway, and then uses the returned receipt and observation to decide what to do next (Fig. 4). The model retains authority over planning and recovery; the harness supplies measurements, enforces the execution boundary, and records what occurred. This section first formalizes the decision process (Sec. 3.1), then describes the three system layers (Sec. 3.2), the explicit task belief maintained by the model (Sec. 3.3), and the three feedback loops that connect planning to execution (Sec. 3.4). Sec. 4 details execution preview and verification through the admission gateway, and Sec. 5 specifies the perception and action interfaces.

3.1 Manipulation as Closed-Loop Decision Making

For each benchmark episode, the model must construct a procedure from the task description and the evidence gathered during that episode; no task-specific solution is prepared in advance. Consequently, each decision uses the information available so far, and each outcome must be returned in a form that can inform the next decision.

Formulation. A case specifies a task description gg and an initial world state s0s_{0} (Sec. 2.1). The world state sts_{t} is hidden from the model, which instead receives observations oto_{t} comprising calibrated multi-view RGB images and the measured robot state. At decision step tt, a pretrained model with fixed parameters θ\theta selects a tool call

ut∼πθ(⋅∣g,Bt,Et),u_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid g,B_{t},E_{t}), (1)

where BtB_{t} is its task belief (Sec. 3.3) and EtE_{t} is the episode’s evidence record, the interactions accumulated so far. The available calls have two roles. Deliberative calls ut∈𝒰du_{t}\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{d}} inspect the scene, measure quantities, compute, retrieve records, revise the belief, or preview a motion. They return a result ete_{t} while leaving the world unchanged:

st+1=st,Et+1=Et∪{(ut,et)}.s_{t+1}=s_{t},\qquad E_{t+1}=E_{t}\cup\{(u_{t},e_{t})\}. (2)

For example, before hanging a mug, the model can localize the mug and rack, inspect the handle orientation, and preview a grasp without advancing simulated time. Physical calls ut∈𝒰pu_{t}\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{p}} request robot motion or the passage of simulated time. They reach the world only through the admission gateway, written as the operator 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which executes an admissible request and returns a receipt rtr_{t} and a fresh observation:

(st+1,rt,ot+1)=𝒜⁡(st,ut),Et+1=Et∪{(ut,rt,ot+1)}.(s_{t+1},r_{t},o_{t+1})=\mathcal{A}(s_{t},u_{t}),\qquad E_{t+1}=E_{t}\cup\{(u_{t},r_{t},o_{t+1})\}. (3)

If 𝒜\mathcal{A} rejects a request, the world remains unchanged and the receipt reports the reason. The model parameters θ\theta, tool set, and task-independent operating guidance remain fixed throughout an episode; adaptation comes from the evolving BtB_{t} and EtE_{t}. Because the simulation is paused during deliberation, reasoning and deliberative calls consume no simulated time.

Quantitative error feedback. A physical request specifies both an intended result and the required precision. Each stage kk has a target x^k\hat{x}_{k} and a model-chosen tolerance τk\tau_{k} (Sec. 5.2). During execution, 𝒜\mathcal{A} measures the reached state xkx_{k} and halts when the deviation ϵk=xk−x^k\epsilon_{k}=x_{k}-\hat{x}_{k} leaves τk\tau_{k}. The resulting receipt reports the completed stages, measured deviations, active tolerance, and unexecuted stages (Sec. 4.2). Thus, if a grasp approach in hang_mugs stops short or the gripper opening differs from the expected value, the model receives the measured discrepancy rather than a generic failure flag. It can then decide whether to inspect the scene, revise the approach, or execute the remaining stages; 𝒜\mathcal{A} does not choose the recovery.

Information boundary. The harness exposes only the published task text, calibrated RGB images, the robot’s measured state, and the public robot model and camera calibration. From these inputs, it may compute learned depth, per-object 3D estimates, and point clouds, reporting each as an estimate with its reliability (Sec. 5.1). The model and its tools cannot access simulator depth, hidden object poses, contact state, or evaluator internals. The benchmark evaluator, rather than the model’s own assessment, determines task success.

3.2 Separating Decision, Capability, and Admission

Auriga separates task reasoning from measurement and execution so that a general-purpose model can build a procedure while every physical action remains reviewable.

Division of responsibility. The harness is organized into three layers (Fig. 4): a model session that makes every task decision, a capability layer of general tools, and an admission gateway that is the only path to the robot. Each layer has a distinct responsibility:

  • •

    Cortex is one persistent model session for the entire episode. It receives task-independent operating guidance, the official task text, and the robot’s capabilities and coordinate conventions. It chooses task decompositions, measurements, action targets, and recovery steps without human intervention or a task-specific prompt, program, or skill.

  • •

    The capability layer provides general tools to measure, act, compute, and recall (Tab. 3). For hang_mugs, these tools can estimate mug and rack locations, compare views, preview a grasp, or retrieve an earlier receipt; they do not encode a solution for hanging mugs.

  • •

    The admission gateway implements 𝒜\mathcal{A}. It is the only path that moves the robot. It receives a reviewed physical request, determines whether the request is admissible, monitors execution, and records the outcome.

One-step dataflow. At each decision step, the model first gathers the evidence needed for the next choice through the capability layer (Sec. 5.1). It then submits either a complete multi-stage action sequence or a program that requests one (Sec. 5.2). Both routes converge on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, so a program-generated motion is previewed and reviewed in the same way as a direct request (Sec. 4.1). After a physical call, the harness stores the reviewed request, receipt, observations before and after execution, and measured displacement in one interaction record (Sec. 5.1). These records make completed motion, normal program termination, and benchmark success separately observable instead of conflating them.

Transparent execution. The model sets task decomposition, targets, and the need for additional evidence; the harness exposes the thresholds that admit, pause, or stop an action and reports their effects. Every physical request, whether direct or program-generated, follows the same admission path. The harness neither substitutes a task-specific rule nor silently changes a parameter supplied by the model. The records constitute EtE_{t}, remain outside the model context, and can be retrieved on demand (Sec. 5.1). The model may attach short operation lessons to them, but it rechecks each lesson against the current scene before using it.

3.3 Deliberation over an Explicit Task Belief

Long-horizon manipulation accumulates observations, receipts, and intermediate decisions. Without a compact representation of the current task understanding, a model can lose track of an earlier objective or confuse an issued command with a verified outcome. Auriga therefore maintains a revisable task belief BtB_{t} alongside the detailed evidence record EtE_{t}.

Structure. The belief has three concise components. The plan records the model’s current understanding of the goal, its intended approach, and the visible evidence that would indicate completion. The attention list records the uncertainties that matter now, the evidence that could resolve each one, and the part of the procedure that depends on it. The ledger records a small number of task-critical premises. Each premise includes an expected event, a status (pending, supported, contradicted, or unknown), the permitted evidence for that status, and the next observation or action that could change it (the labeled premises in Fig. 1). The harness admits no physical action until the model has submitted a belief.

For example, in hang_mugs, the plan can state “grasp the mug by its handle, lift it, and place it on the rack hook.” An attention item can require a view that resolves the handle orientation before the approach. A ledger premise can state that the mug is retained by the gripper: it is initially pending, and becomes supported only after permitted evidence, such as the expected gripper opening together with a confirming lift observation, is available.

Belief versus evidence. BtB_{t} is a compact, revisable working state rather than an action script or a source of evidence. Concrete poses, arm timing, and gripper commands remain part of individual actions, so the model can change them as new measurements arrive. Likewise, a belief entry must be checked against fresh observations before it supports a decision: a closed gripper alone does not verify that a mug is retained. When the conversation is compacted to fit the context window, the harness reinserts the latest BtB_{t} as the model’s provisional judgment, while the details of earlier interactions remain retrievable from EtE_{t}.

3.4 Closing the Loop at Three Time Scales

Errors can arise within a movement, between successive actions, or only after a task-level premise has been tested. Auriga addresses these cases with three nested loops that have distinct responsibilities: the admission gateway stops unsafe or off-target execution, while the model diagnoses the result and chooses the recovery. Fig. 5 shows how the three loops interleave within one episode.

Stage loop. Within a single action, 𝒜\mathcal{A} contains errors: applying the stage check of Sec. 3.1 during execution, it halts at the first stage whose deviation ϵk\epsilon_{k} leaves τk\tau_{k}, and also pauses at a failed grasp check or at a checkpoint placed by the model (Sec. 4.2). For a hang_mugs grasp, it can stop the sequence immediately when the measured gripper opening indicates that the mug handle was not secured. The stage loop keeps an error from propagating to later stages; it does not repair the motion.

Action loop. Between actions, the model diagnoses outcomes: after each physical call, it compares the receipt and fresh observation with its intended result and forms a cause hypothesis before acting again. It may continue the remaining previewed stages, replan from the stopped stage without repeating completed stages, change the contact, route, target, arm, or tolerance, or collect an observation that distinguishes competing explanations. For example, after an unsuccessful mug grasp, the model can inspect whether the handle orientation, approach route, or target localization caused the discrepancy before choosing a new approach. Whenever possible, normal task progress tests the hypothesis; a separate probe is used only when its result would alter the next decision.

Belief loop. Across the episode, the model revises its premises: action outcomes update the ledger and, when necessary, the plan in BtB_{t}. If repeated evidence contradicts a premise, the model changes its task-level explanation and selects a different mechanism, such as another contact, route, or target, rather than simply restating the same hypothesis. In hang_mugs, evidence that a top-down approach repeatedly fails can update the belief so that the model seeks a handle-oriented grasp or a different approach route. This loop keeps the model’s working understanding aligned with the evidence accumulated during the episode. Sec. 4 next describes the admission path in which the stage loop runs.

4 Admission Gateway: Preview and Verification

To close the planning–execution gap quantified in Secs. 2.2 and 2, Auriga binds physical execution to a trajectory preview that the model can inspect before committing (Sec. 4.1) and verifies the measured state as the trajectory runs (Sec. 4.2). Auriga follows a single rule, enforced by the admission operator 𝒜\mathcal{A}: the motion that reaches the robot is exactly the motion compiled into its preview, and whenever execution departs from it beyond the declared tolerance, the harness stops and reports the measured state rather than repairing it on the model’s behalf.

4.1 Preview Before Acting

Preview gives the model a first guarantee, namely that every motion, whether requested by the model or by a program it has written, is compiled into a preview before it runs, and that nothing else is executed. The model reviews this preview by default and can skip the review to save a call. Below, we describe how the model sees a motion and how execution is held to it.

Seeing the whole motion. Rather than issuing one movement per call, the model describes a complete action sequence for one arm or for both arms at once, such as approaching an object, closing the gripper, lifting, transporting, and releasing it. The harness plans the entire sequence into a robot trajectory before anything moves and returns a preview of what would happen. Any adjustment the harness makes to how a movement is realized happens at this stage, so the preview already shows the motion that will run. The preview draws the planned gripper paths (Fig. 6) and arm configurations on the camera image and reports how long each part of the sequence would take on each arm. It also estimates the clearance between the robot, the objects it holds, and the obstacles the model has declared, such as whether the two arms come close to each other. Such estimates are given as advice, and the decision whether to proceed stays with the model. If any part of the sequence cannot be planned, nothing is executed, and the preview states which part failed and why.

Committing to it. Once the model accepts a preview, the harness replays the previewed trajectory without replanning it. Because the simulation is paused while the model inspects the preview, the robot is still in the state from which the preview was planned, and looking ahead costs no execution time. The robot therefore performs the previewed motion, so every later report refers to a motion the model can inspect. In free space the robot follows the previewed trajectory closely, which means that a deviation during execution almost always indicates contact, the case that Sec. 4.2 is built around.

4.2 Verify While Acting

Preview fixes what will be executed, but not how the world will respond. Contact, slip, and objects displaced by earlier actions can still make the outcome differ from the plan. Verification gives the second guarantee, namely that every divergence of the robot from its previewed motion beyond the tolerance is caught at the end of the movement in which it occurs and handed back to the model together with the facts needed to act on it.

Catching divergence. After each movement, the harness compares where the gripper actually is with where the preview placed it. The tolerance τk\tau_{k} of a movement (Sec. 3.1) consists of a position part δp\delta_{p} and an orientation part δθ\delta_{\theta}. The model can set both for each movement, by default δp=10\delta_{p}{=}10 mm and δθ=0.15\delta_{\theta}{=}0.15 rad. If the difference exceeds the tolerance set for that movement, the robot stops and holds its pose instead of continuing with the rest of the sequence. The receipt rtr_{t} that follows states which movement failed, by how much it missed, and which parts did not run. It also adds a fresh camera view from the stopping point and images of the measured and the previewed route. Movements that already completed are kept rather than undone. In Fig. 6, a finger lands on a basket rim while the object is lowered, and the measured path leaves the previewed one beyond its tolerance. The harness stops the arm and reports only this miss, and the model identifies the rim as the cause from the fresh view. It then previews a revised motion that clears the rim, which completes the placement in a second round. This check targets the main source of divergence, contact with an object or fixture, which the planner does not model, so the harness detects its consequence instead of predicting it.

Looking where the model chooses. Some divergences leave the robot on its planned path and show only in the scene, such as an object that slips or shifts during a grasp. The model can therefore insert checkpoints at moments it considers critical, either unconditionally or only when the measured gripper opening after a grasp falls outside the range it expects, for example when the fingers close on nothing. At a checkpoint the robot stops and the model receives a fresh view, after which it either continues the remaining sequence as previewed or replaces it. In Fig. 6, the model places a checkpoint after the lift, and the sequence continues as previewed once the fresh wrist view shows the object still held. Checkpoints are placed by the model rather than at fixed points, since pausing after every gripper action by default fragmented long tasks. Acting on what a stop or a checkpoint reveals, however, often requires facts that the model cannot read reliably from RGB, such as whether an object is held and where it sits relative to the gripper, which the following section provides.

5 Capability Layer: Perception and Action Interfaces

Faithful execution helps only if the motion the model chooses is the right one, which depends on what the model can perceive and on how it can express what it wants. A general-purpose vision-language model reads a scene and plans a task well, but it is weak at the quantitative side of manipulation. This section describes how the harness compensates on both sides, by turning physical state into facts the model can read (Sec. 5.1) and by letting the model state its intent in terms of the task (Sec. 5.2), as summarized in Fig. 7. Two principles guide both sides. The harness informs but does not decide, reporting measurements and estimates together with how reliable they are and leaving the choice of what to do with them to the model. It also attaches facts at the point of decision, so that information that should change the next command arrives with the preview or the report instead of waiting to be requested.

5.1 Readable Physical State

On the input side, every quantity the model needs for its next decision reaches it as a measured, computed, or estimated fact together with how reliable it is, rather than as something the model has to infer from pixels. We describe how the model locates things, learns what an action did, and recalls what happened earlier.

3D localization. The model understands the layout of a scene well from RGB, but an image does not show metric 3D positions directly, so any estimate made from appearance alone remains uncertain. A deployed robot, however, comes with physical quantities that are known exactly, namely the intrinsic and extrinsic calibration of every camera, the height of the work surface, and the kinematic model of the robot itself. With the calibration, every pixel (u,v)(u,v) of a camera with intrinsics KK, orientation RR, and center 𝐜\mathbf{c} lies on a known ray with direction 𝐝=R​K−1​(u,v,1)⊤\mathbf{d}=R\,K^{-1}(u,v,1)^{\top}, so locating it in 3D reduces to finding its distance along this ray. The harness provides two tools that supply this distance at different levels of precision (Fig. 7a). The first estimates every visible object in 3D. VGGT-Omega [46] predicts a depth for every pixel of the head-camera image, which places the pixel on its ray, and the depths are scaled so that the table lies at its known height. SAM 3.1 [2] separates the objects in these points, and each object is reported with its 3D position, orientation, and size and with how reliable the estimate is, in every full observation and every action report. Where such an estimate is not precise enough, as for placing the fingers on a narrow edge, the second tool computes the position of a point that the model selects in an image. The model fixes its distance either with a plane 𝐧⊤​𝐩=h\mathbf{n}^{\top}\mathbf{p}=h of known height,

𝐩=𝐜+h−𝐧⊤​𝐜𝐧⊤​𝐝​𝐝,∂𝐩∂h=𝐝𝐧⊤​𝐝,\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{c}+\frac{h-\mathbf{n}^{\top}\mathbf{c}}{\mathbf{n}^{\top}\mathbf{d}}\,\mathbf{d},\qquad\frac{\partial\mathbf{p}}{\partial h}=\frac{\mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{n}^{\top}\mathbf{d}}, (4)

or by marking the same point in a second view, such as the wrist camera, from which the harness triangulates it. The two tools meet in the plane height. For a point on the table, the height is known exactly. For a point on an object, the model either takes the height from the learned depth of that object, in which case the harness reports how far the point would move if this height were off, or marks the point in a second view, which needs no height. Any 3D point, including the fingers placed by the kinematic model, can be projected back into the image to check it.

Action outcomes and in-hand state. After an action, the model needs its physical outcome. For most of the scene, the next image shows it, and each report also lists the objects whose estimated position changed during the action. A grasp is harder, since the fingers often hide the object, so the image may not show the state of the object and how it interacts with the gripper. The harness therefore complements the image with measurements of both. For the gripper, every report includes its measured opening. For the object, the model can measure on request where a visible part of it, such as its lower end, lies relative to the gripper, the axis of the object in the 3D points around the fingers, and how far a part marked in a wrist image before an action has moved after it. The object estimates also keep the pose that the object had in the hand at the grasp, as a reference for these measurements. Together, these tell the model whether the object is held, how it sits in the hand, and whether it has turned or slipped since the grasp.

Episode history and warnings. In long episodes the context is compacted and early images are dropped, while recovery often depends on what earlier attempts actually achieved. The model can therefore retrieve from the evidence record EtE_{t} (Sec. 3.1) any earlier camera frame, including a magnified region of it, a list of past actions with the displacement that each one measured, and the planned and measured trajectories of any action. Full history is retrieved on demand rather than pushed into every turn, since forced reviews of history produced idle calls. The exception is history that bears directly on the next command. A report of a stopped or failed action carries a short summary of recent outcomes, and a preview that returns to a place where a motion has failed carries a warning, so that the model does not unknowingly repeat a failed attempt.

5.2 Expressive Actions

On the output side, the model states what it wants in terms of the task, such as where the fingers should touch and how the two arms should cooperate, and the harness turns these statements into motion. We describe how the model specifies the goal of each movement and how it sets the timing and speed of a sequence.

Finger-referenced goals. A robot interface typically takes the pose of the wrist as its goal, whereas what matters for a task is where the fingers touch the object and how precisely they get there. In Auriga, each movement states its goal in these terms. The model gives where the gripper should end up and how it should be turned in a frame fixed to the workspace, together with the part of the fingers that should make contact, such as the fingertip or the pad center, so that the goal refers to the point that touches the object rather than to the wrist. It also states how precisely the gripper must arrive, so that a tight insertion and a coarse transit are checked differently.

Shared timeline and speed. Goals alone do not fix how a sequence unfolds in time. When both arms take part, or when a movement passes from free space to contact, the order and the speed of its parts matter as much as its goals. In Auriga, the stages of both arms belong to the same sequence and advance on a shared timeline. Stages of the two arms run at the same time unless the model declares that one must wait for another. The model also sets the speed of each movement, typically slower near contact, and can let the gripper open or close during a movement, for example opening it on the way to an object. Speed and gripper timing are fixed in the preview like the path itself, so they are part of the reviewed motion.

6 Experiments

We evaluate Auriga under the zero-shot protocol of Sec. 2.1 on two simulation benchmarks: dual-arm tabletop manipulation on RoboDojo [4] (Sec. 6.1.1) and kitchen mobile manipulation on RoboCasa365 [32] (Sec. 6.1.2). After describing the experimental setup (Sec. 6.1), we report main results on RoboDojo (Sec. 6.2) and RoboCasa365 (Sec. 6.3), mechanism ablations (Sec. 6.4), execution efficiency and tool usage (Sec. 6.5), and qualitative behavior and failure modes (Sec. 6.6).

6.1 Experimental Setup

6.1.1 RoboDojo

RoboDojo [4] simulates a dual-arm ARX X5 robot with one head camera and two wrist cameras in Isaac Sim.

Capability dimensions. RoboDojo groups its 42 tasks into five capability dimensions: Generalization (12 tasks, each with standard and random scenes), Precision (8), Long-Horizon (8), Memory (6), and Open (8); Tab. 13 in App. A lists what each dimension covers and its tasks. As on the official leaderboard, results are first averaged across the tasks of each dimension and then across the five dimensions, with equal weight at both levels. For Generalization, the value of each task and of the dimension is the equal-weight mean of its standard-scene average and its random-scene average.

Evaluation set. Following Sec. 2.1, a case specifies a task, a scene variant (standard or random), an evaluation seed, and a layout, and an episode is one execution of a case by the agent. The evaluation set follows the protocol of the official leaderboard, with three evaluation seeds and, in each seed, 50 cases for each of the 42 tasks, that is, 2,100 cases per seed and 6,300 in all. In each seed, every Generalization task contributes 25 cases with standard scenes and 25 with random scenes, and every other task contributes 50 with standard scenes. Each case counts with its first official score, including scores of zero, and any later episode of the same case is ignored. When an infrastructure fault ends an episode before the evaluator has scored it, the case is re-run under the same configuration.

Metrics. SR is the share of cases that the benchmark evaluator judges fully successful, over a fixed denominator: a case without an official score stays in the denominator and does not count as a success. Score is the official graded process score of the evaluator, from 0 to 100, averaged over the cases with an official score. Both metrics are first computed for each task in each seed, and a task’s value is the mean of its three per-seed values; the dimension values and the five-dimension average then follow from the task values as in Sec. 6.1.1. Steps are the native steps that the simulator executes in an episode, also reported as a percentage of the official native-step limit of the task, which ranges from 200 to 1,900 steps; a single action request may use at most 250 steps. Calls are the model calls (the model responses in an episode) and the direct tool calls issued by the model; tool calls issued by model-written programs are counted separately. Cost comprises the input tokens of the model session (total, share served from the prompt cache in %, and uncached input tokens), the output tokens, and the wall-clock time of the episode; Steps, Calls, and Cost are reported as means per episode.

Agent configuration. The RoboDojo results (Secs. 6.2, 6.5 and 6.5) use Auriga as described in Secs. 3, 4 and 5, with the model gpt-6-astra at reasoning effort high. An episode may use at most 170 model responses and the official native-step limit of its task, and the simulation is paused while the model deliberates (Sec. 3.1). The model observes RGB images from the three cameras, proprioception, and the public camera calibration, together with the object estimates that the harness computes from the head-camera image (Sec. 5.1); simulator depth and hidden object state are withheld. Its task text is the native instruction of the task, the official task page with its description and scoring rules, and the task-independent operating guidance of the harness (Secs. 3.1 and 3.2). The ablations in Sec. 6.4 remove or restrict individual mechanisms of this configuration while keeping the rest fixed.

6.1.2 RoboCasa365

RoboCasa365 [32] evaluates household mobile manipulation with a single Franka Panda arm mounted on an Omron mobile base across kitchen environments, spanning 365 tasks (65 atomic and 300 composite).

Tasks and task groups. Evaluation focuses on the benchmark’s 50 Target50 tasks, organized into three groups: 18 Atomic-Seen tasks involving single manipulation skills (e.g., opening a drawer or operating a microwave); 16 Composite-Seen tasks that chain two to fifteen subtasks whose templates appear in the benchmark’s pretraining demonstrations; and 16 Composite-Unseen tasks of comparable horizon whose templates are absent from the pretraining demonstrations.

Evaluation protocol and metrics. Whereas the standard policy leaderboard [40] evaluates demonstration-trained policies in the 2,500 pretraining kitchens, agent evaluations are conducted in ten unseen target kitchens with novel layouts, fixtures, and objects. We follow the protocol of the published agent baselines [61, 43]: every task is evaluated at seeds 1–5, giving 250 episodes (90 Atomic-Seen, 80 Composite-Seen, and 80 Composite-Unseen). We report the success rate (SR, %) of each group, of all 160 composite episodes, and Overall as the mean over the 50 tasks, which equals the SR over all 250 episodes. The benchmark environment provides camera images, robot proprioception, world-coordinate maps derived from rendered depth, the source code of the task’s success check, and live values of the predicates tested by that check.

Baselines. Both published agent baselines plan with an LLM agent and hand contact-rich phases, such as grasping an object or turning a knob, to the RLDX-1 vision-language-action (VLA) policy [17]. RPent [61] also retrieves task memory, built by exploring each task on seed 0 before evaluation. PyRUA-Lean [43] uses no cross-episode memory. We also list RLDX-1 on its own and, as in the comparison of RPent, three learned policies evaluated in the pretraining kitchens.

Agent configuration. Auriga runs gpt-6-astra at high reasoning effort with at most 100 model requests per episode. Unlike both agent baselines, it uses no VLA policy and no cross-episode memory. Alongside the benchmark-provided observations and task predicates, Auriga segments camera images via SAM 3.1 [2] from model-chosen text prompts and projects each mask onto the world coordinate map, without reading ground-truth object poses. All physical motions are executed through multi-stage action programs under the preview-and-verification gateway of Sec. 4, coordinating stages for the arm, gripper, torso, and mobile base.

6.2 Main Results on RoboDojo

Tab. 4 places Auriga on the official leaderboard [41], reporting Score and SR on average and in each dimension. The table has two blocks: the eight leading entries that use a learned policy, either a world action model (WAM) or a vision-language-action (VLA) policy, alone or with an agent; and four agent methods, which act through tools or code, together with Auriga. Averaged across the five dimensions, Auriga reaches a Score of 64.00 and an SR of 57.74%. Across both blocks of Tab. 4, Auriga achieves the highest overall averages, ahead of GO-3 Nano Preview, which combines an agent with a world action model, at 61.90 and 56.42%. Within the agent block, Auriga leads all twelve columns, including both averages (ahead of PyRUA-Lean at 55.26 and 50.35%). According to their reports [43, 11, 20, 60], PyRUA-Lean, HexaShell-Preview, EmbodiedEvo, and RoboProbe all use gpt-6-astra, the same base model as Auriga (marked † in Tab. 4), with reasoning effort high for PyRUA-Lean, xhigh for EmbodiedEvo, and medium for RoboProbe; Auriga uses high. Against RoboProbe [60], the reference harness released with the evaluation of GPT-6 Astra on RoboDojo [4], Auriga raises the average Score from 28.97 to 64.00 and the average SR from 22.48% to 57.74% on the same model (Tab. 4).

By dimension. Across both blocks of Tab. 4, Auriga has the highest Score and SR in Generalization, Memory, and Open, ahead of the next entry by 5.72, 11.99, and 4.83 percentage points in SR. Precision and Long-Horizon remain the most challenging dimensions for Auriga, at 38.50% and 45.24% SR, against 76.00% and 53.50% for GO-3 Nano Preview, which leads both, though Auriga ranks second overall in both Score and SR across Precision (46.30 and 38.50%) and Long-Horizon (62.10 and 45.24%).

Profile against other methods. Fig. 8 compares the five-dimension profile of Auriga with seven other methods of Tab. 4: the four highest-scoring entries of the WAM / VLA block (GO-3 Nano Preview, WorldScape-R2SI, WALL-OSS-1.0-lite, and VPP2) and the three highest-scoring other entries of the agent block (PyRUA-Lean, HexaShell-Preview, and EmbodiedEvo); Fig. 20 in App. D plots the same values as bars, together with RoboProbe. GO-3 Nano Preview has the opposite profile to Auriga: its Score exceeds that of Auriga by 32.35 in Precision and 6.11 in Long-Horizon, while falling below Auriga in the other three dimensions, most in Memory (64.50 vs. 93.40) and Generalization (36.45 vs. 52.90). Against PyRUA-Lean, Auriga achieves a higher Score in all five dimensions, with gains of 1.53 in Precision, 4.63 in Generalization, 4.84 in Open, 7.80 in Long-Horizon, and 25.00 in Memory.

Per task. Tabs. 18 and 21 in App. E compare Auriga task by task with PyRUA-Lean, HexaShell-Preview, EmbodiedEvo, and RoboProbe. Against each of the four, Auriga is higher in Score on more of the 42 tasks than it is lower, from 24 vs. 17 tasks against PyRUA-Lean to 41 vs. 1 against RoboProbe. In SR, it is likewise higher on more tasks against all four methods: PyRUA-Lean (22 vs. 16), HexaShell-Preview (28 vs. 9), EmbodiedEvo (32 vs. 6), and RoboProbe (38 vs. 1).

Generalization under randomization. Fig. 9 compares the entries of Tab. 4 on the 12 Generalization tasks across the standard and random scenes, reporting the SR change Δ​SR=SRrand−SRstd\Delta\text{SR}=\text{SR}_{\mathrm{rand}}-\text{SR}_{\mathrm{std}} in panel (a) and the composite generalization metric G=12​(Sstd+Srand)−|Srand−Sstd|G=\tfrac{1}{2}(S_{\mathrm{std}}+S_{\mathrm{rand}})-|S_{\mathrm{rand}}-S_{\mathrm{std}}| in panel (b), which rewards a high mean Score and penalizes the gap between the two scene types (Tab. 17 in App. D lists the SR and Score on both scene types). Auriga achieves the highest GG in Fig. 9 at 46.27, ahead of PyRUA-Lean at 43.87 and WorldScape-R2SI at 35.61. Across both scene types, Auriga achieves the highest SR and Score of all 13 entries: 52.28% SR and 56.22 Score on the standard scenes, and 45.61% SR and 49.58 Score on the random scenes, with a change of −6.7-6.7 percentage points in SR (−13%-13\% relative) and −6.6-6.6 points in Score (Tab. 17). By contrast, the learned WAM and VLA entries suffer steep drops under scene randomization, losing up to 33.933.9 percentage points in SR (31.531.5 points in Score) for VPP2 and 18.718.7 percentage points (−43%-43\% relative) for GO-3 Nano Preview (Figs. 9 and 17).

6.3 Main Results on RoboCasa365

RoboCasa365 shifts the evaluation to a mobile manipulator operating doors, drawers, knobs, and appliances across unseen kitchens over chains of up to fifteen subtasks (Sec. 6.1.2). Tabs. 5 and 10 compare Auriga with the published agent baselines and with RLDX-1 on the 250 Target50 episodes (Sec. 6.1.2). All three agent methods use gpt-6-astra at high reasoning effort, and the baseline results are those reported by RPent [61] and PyRUA-Lean [43]. As in the comparison of RPent, Tab. 5 also lists WorldDreamer, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and π0\pi_{0}, which are evaluated in the pretraining kitchens; for these policies, Composite All is the mean of the two composite groups. These policies, together with the leaderboard entry Xiaomi-Robotics-1, are also listed in Tab. 15 in App. C.

Comparison with agent baselines. Auriga succeeds in 73.2% of the 250 episodes, against 59.2% for RPent and 56.4% for PyRUA-Lean with the same model and reasoning effort, and 30.0% for RLDX-1 alone. It has the highest success rate in every group of Tab. 5. The margin is largest on the composite tasks, which chain several subtasks: Auriga completes 62.5% of these episodes, 19.4 percentage points more than RPent and 23.1 more than PyRUA-Lean. Both baselines rely on the RLDX-1 policy for contact-rich phases, and RPent also on task memory gathered before evaluation; Auriga uses neither.

Where Auriga gains and where it fails. The composite gap reflects how contact-rich phases are executed. The baselines hand them to RLDX-1, which on its own completes 21.3% of the Composite-Seen and 5.0% of the Composite-Unseen tasks, while Auriga builds every phase, including grasps, placements, and fixture operations, from action programs whose stages are checked as they execute (Sec. 4). Of the 67 failed episodes of Auriga, 23 ended when the 100 model requests were used and 44 after the model stopped acting for several turns (Fig. 19 in App. C). Four composite tasks fail in all five episodes, PackIdenticalLunches and StoreLeftoversInBowl among the seen and MakeIceLemonade and SeparateFreezerRack among the unseen, while every Atomic-Seen task succeeds in at least three of its five episodes.

6.4 Ablation Studies

Whereas Fig. 3 (Sec. 2.3) tracked the cumulative gains across development iterations, Tabs. 6 to 10 isolate the contribution of each mechanism of Secs. 3, 4 and 5 on the frozen configuration of Sec. 6.1.1. Each table groups related mechanisms and evaluates its variants on ten tasks (Tab. 14 in App. B): Tabs. 6 to 9 on five standard layouts of each task (50 cases), and Tab. 10 on 30 cases. Each variant removes or restricts the mechanisms marked in its row while keeping the rest of the configuration fixed, and the Full row reports the main configuration on the same cases. Alongside the number of successes and the mean Score, each table reports a mechanism-specific diagnostic per episode for the ablated variants (and for all rows in Tab. 10), taken from the execution receipts rtr_{t}, the evidence record EtE_{t}, or the model calls (Secs. 3.1 and 3.2).

Spatial measurement. Tab. 6 evaluates the mechanisms that provide metric 3D positions (Sec. 5.1): the camera calibration and 3D object estimates, together with geometry_query for ray–plane intersection (equation 4), two-view triangulation, and 3D-to-image projection. In No geometry tools, the calibration, the 3D object estimates, and geometry_query are all removed, so the model locates targets from the RGB images and the robot state alone (Sec. 5.1). In No triangulation, the calibration, the 3D object estimates, two-view triangulation, and 3D-to-image projection are removed while ray–plane intersection (equation 4) remains available at one plane height per pixel. Compared with Full (46/50 successes, mean Score 94.9), No geometry tools reaches 30/50 successes and a Score of 67.1, with 65.3% of first grasps held. With ray–plane intersection available, No triangulation reaches 40/50 successes and a Score of 84.0, with 85.7% of first grasps held; Full adds two-view triangulation, 3D-to-image projection, the calibration, and the 3D object estimates (Sec. 5.1).

Collision handling. Tab. 7 evaluates two mechanisms that keep execution clear of unintended contact (Secs. 4.1 and 4.2). In No clearance review, the preview no longer estimates the clearance between the arms, held objects, and declared obstacles before motion (Sec. 4.1). In No divergence stop, the stage loop in 𝒜\mathcal{A} no longer halts the sequence when a movement exceeds its arrival tolerance τk=(δp,δθ)\tau_{k}=(\delta_{p},\delta_{\theta}), so later stages continue from the displaced pose (Secs. 3.4 and 4.2). Compared with Full (36/50 successes, Score 79.8), No clearance review reaches 31/50 and 69.1, with 1.20 tolerance stops per episode; without the clearance review, the stage check during execution is the remaining guard against contact (Sec. 4.2). Compared with Full, No divergence stop reaches 34/50 and 75.1, with 0.00 stops and 0.92 out-of-tolerance movements per episode as sequences run on, whereas stage verification in Full halts at the first exceeded tolerance and returns a receipt rtr_{t} and fresh view (Secs. 3.4 and 4.2).

Preview and checkpoints. Tab. 8 evaluates two mechanisms of the admission operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} (Secs. 3.2 and 4): previewing a trajectory before execution (Sec. 4.1) and pausing only at model-placed checkpoints (Sec. 4.2). In No preview, an action request is planned and executed in one call, so the model sees the trajectory only after it has run (Sec. 4.1). In Pause after every gripper action, 𝒜\mathcal{A} inserts a checkpoint after every gripper stage that a later movement depends on, rather than only where the model placed one (Sec. 4.2). Compared with Full (42/50 successes, Score 88.5), No preview reaches 36/50 and 74.7, with 0.96 checkpoint pauses and 4.31 unreviewed motions per episode, 0.98 of which carry a clearance risk that preview reports before motion (Sec. 4.1). Compared with Full, Pause after every gripper action reaches 37/50 and 78.7 with 13.82 pauses per episode, whereas model-placed checkpoints in Full pause only at stages selected for inspection (Sec. 4.2).

Expressive actions. Tab. 9 evaluates the two output-side mechanisms of Sec. 5.2: finger-referenced movement goals and the shared dual-arm timeline. In Wrist-flange goals, each movement specifies the wrist-flange position and quaternion rather than a finger contact point and workspace rotations (Sec. 5.2), and the overlay that projects the finger positions into the image (Sec. 5.1) is removed. In One arm at a time, an action request may contain stages for only one arm, so the two arms no longer advance on a shared timeline (Sec. 5.2). Compared with Full (39/50 successes, Score 83.9), Wrist-flange goals reaches 37/50 and 77.1 with 3.42 unplannable stages per episode, whereas finger-referenced goals in Full let the model specify the finger contact region and workspace orientation directly (Sec. 5.2). Compared with Full, One arm at a time reaches 35/50 and 74.8 with 1.14 unplannable stages per episode, whereas the shared timeline in Full coordinates both arms with declared waits in one sequence (Sec. 5.2).

Programs. Tab. 10 evaluates how model-written programs interact with 𝒜\mathcal{A} (Secs. 3.2 and 4.1): in Full, a program computes and calls deliberative tools (𝒰d\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{d}}) freely, while any physical request (𝒰p\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{p}}) enters 𝒜\mathcal{A}, waits for the model to review its preview (Sec. 4.1), and returns a receipt rtr_{t} (Secs. 3.1 and 3.2). In No programs, the Compute capability (program_run, Tab. 3) is removed, so the model issues every call directly. In Programs cannot act, programs still run for computation and deliberative queries, but 𝒜\mathcal{A} rejects their physical requests, so the model issues every physical action directly (Sec. 3.2). In Code as policy, physical requests from a program run without preview review and return no receipts rtr_{t} to the program or the model, leaving only the program’s output and exit status, as in the paradigm contrasted with Auriga in Secs. 2.2 and 3.2. Compared with Full (30/30 successes, Score 100.0, 46.2 model calls per episode), No programs reaches 19/30 and 75.3 with 66.0 calls per episode (one episode exhausting the 170-response limit), and Programs cannot act reaches 19/30 and 73.0 with 67.1 calls per episode; in Full, programs issue 28.8 tool calls per episode while the model executes 5.9 physical actions directly (Sec. 3.2). Compared with Full, Code as policy reaches 20/30 and 77.2 with 71.8 calls per episode. Its programs issue 120 physical actions over the 30 episodes, of which 2 halt when a movement exceeds its arrival tolerance and 1 stops at a checkpoint; without receipts rtr_{t}, each of these programs still exits with code 0, one of them after issuing 8 further actions (Secs. 4.2 and 3.2).

6.5 Execution Efficiency and Tool Usage

Episode cost across methods and dimensions. Of the other methods in Tab. 4, PyRUA-Lean [43], HexaShell-Preview [11], and EmbodiedEvo [20] report the test-episode cost of their RoboDojo runs. Tab. 11 lists the cost per test episode of these three methods and of Auriga (measured over the 6,299 scored episodes of Tab. 16), together with each method’s overall average Score in Tab. 4. Of the methods that report input tokens, Auriga achieves the highest average Score (64.00) and uses 5.63 million input tokens per episode, of which 85.4% are served from the prompt cache, leaving 0.82 million uncached input tokens per episode (against 3.94 million total and 0.09 million uncached for EmbodiedEvo at 45.08 Score, and 0.75 million total for PyRUA-Lean at 55.26 Score). An Auriga episode averages 47.5 model calls and 18.8 minutes, compared with 25.7 calls and 12.7 minutes for PyRUA-Lean and a median of 12.3 minutes for HexaShell-Preview. Note that cross-trial evolution methods (Tab. 1) also incur pre-evaluation trial costs that are not included in their per-test-episode numbers, whereas Auriga runs entirely within the evaluated episode.

Fig. 11 compares the five-dimension Score of Auriga (Tab. 4) against the mean input tokens and uncached input tokens per episode across dimensions (Tab. 16 in App. D). Memory, the dimension with the highest Score (93.40), is also the cheapest, with 30.0 model calls, 3.11 million input tokens (0.45 million uncached), and 11.3 minutes per episode, and Open, with the second-highest Score (65.40), is the second cheapest, with 40.7 model calls, 4.67 million input tokens (0.65 million uncached), and 14.9 minutes. Long-Horizon and Generalization episodes are the most expensive, with 54.5 and 54.2 model calls, 6.70 and 6.57 million input tokens, and 23.0 and 21.6 minutes, and across all 6,299 episodes Auriga uses 79.7% of the native-step limit on average (Tab. 16).

Tool usage across capabilities and episode progress. Figs. 13 and 13 group the tool calls of the model by the four capabilities of Tab. 3: Measure, Act, Compute, and Recall. An episode makes 38 direct tool calls on average, from 45 in Long-Horizon and Generalization episodes to 23 in Memory episodes (Fig. 13). Act takes the largest share (45%), followed by Measure (24%), Compute (17%), and Recall (15%). Within each capability, spatial measurement (geometry_query) accounts for 16% of all direct tool calls and scene observation (robot_observe, alongside stereo_guide) for 8% under Measure; under Act, trajectory preview (𝒰d\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{d}}, equation 2) accounts for 19% and physical execution (𝒰p\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{p}}, equation 3) for 24% in robot_action (with robot_wait at 2%), so 44% of all robot_action calls preview a candidate sequence without advancing the world; under Compute, running programs (program_run) accounts for 17% (with programs issuing 7 additional tool calls per episode on average, rising to 10 in Long-Horizon); and under Recall, updating the task belief (task_plan, Sec. 3.3) accounts for 13% while querying evidence records (history_* and operation_memory, Sec. 3.2) accounts for 2%. Across normalized episode progress t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] (Fig. 13), Measure takes 87% of calls before t=0.05t=0.05 as the model inspects the scene and localizes targets before acting; from t=0.15t=0.15 onward, Act (46%–54%) and Compute (17%–22%) account for over 60% of calls while Recall stays between 13% and 17%.

Execution granularity against the reference harness. To compare model interaction and physical execution granularity on matched zero-shot scenes, Tab. 12 evaluates Auriga against the published RoboProbe release [60] across the 15 standard-variant scenes of swap_T (full step-by-step execution traces and mechanism statistics are detailed in App. F). Auriga completes 14 of the 15 scenes (93.3% SR), compared with 3 of 15 (20.0% SR) for RoboProbe (+73.3+73.3 percentage points), while using fewer model calls per episode (25.4 vs. 36.6 mean, 24 vs. 38 median). Across the 15 episodes, RoboProbe issues 501 physical execution batches (33.4 per episode, 10.9 native steps per batch), whereas Auriga issues 47 batches (3.1 per episode, 107.3 native steps per batch)—a 90.6% reduction in physical execution invocations for a comparable number of native steps (336.2 vs. 365.1), because approach, grasp, transport, and release are previewed and verified as multi-stage operations rather than single end-effector steps.

6.6 Qualitative Analysis and Failure Modes

We complement the aggregate metrics and ablations with qualitative episode traces across both RoboDojo and RoboCasa365, organized around four operational challenges: recovery after grasp failure and transport slippage (Sec. 6.6), scope-matched replanning and budget-aware preview (Sec. 6.6), 3D geometry-guided manipulation with VGGT-Omega and SAM 3.1 (Sec. 6.6), and failure modes when repeated corrections under multi-body coupling exhaust the episode budget (Sec. 6.6). Full step-by-step trace tables on swap_T and additional case studies are provided in Apps. F and G.

Recovery from grasp failure, transport slippage, and arm handover. Grasp acquisition, retention during transport, and stable support after release are tracked as distinct conditions in the task belief BtB_{t}, allowing the model to revise how an object is grasped or transported without losing already verified subgoals (Fig. 14).

In RoboDojo imitate_sorting_sequence (Fig. 14(a)), the model must reproduce a five-object placement order (wristwatch, black device, rabbit, phone, gold vehicle). After the first two objects are verified inside the basket, the rabbit lies outside the left arm’s reach, so the right arm transfers it toward the center. When the rabbit slips during transfer and lands outside the basket’s far rim, the task belief keeps the third slot marked pending rather than advancing to the phone; after a head grasp catches the rim and triggers a tracking_error stop, the model inspects the wrist view, rotates the jaws across the rabbit’s torso in a clearer region, verifies placement inside the basket, and only then proceeds to the remaining two objects. Similarly, in T-block pose exchange (swap_T, Tab. 19 in App. F), when the blue block slips onto the table during a right-arm transfer whose robot motion nonetheless reports completed with zero final gripper aperture, the model marks blue retention as contradicted while preserving the already placed pink block as supported, switches recovery to the nearby left arm, and completes the exchange to the saved initial pose.

In RoboCasa365 WashLettuce (Fig. 14(b)), transport slippage prompts the model to change the transport mode altogether. After the initial grasp, moving the mobile base causes the head of lettuce to slip onto the counter, as flagged by the execution receipt and wrist-camera object table. When holding the mobile base stationary still leaves three upper-leaf re-grasps blocked or slipping, the model targets a narrower lower section of the lettuce beside the sink and replaces an aerial transfer with a counter-supported slide directly into the basin, before turning on the faucet and pushing the lettuce under the water stream to complete the task (additional slippage recovery cases on pick_from_conveyor_by_image, stack_bowls, and PickPlaceDrawerToCounter are analyzed in App. G).

Scope-matched replanning and budget-aware trajectory preview. When an execution receipt and post-action observation invalidate a physical assumption, the model matches the scope of its revision to the contradicted premise (Fig. 15).

In RoboDojo pack_objects_into_box (Fig. 15(a)), the robot must pack a car, shoe, hammer, and toothbrush into a box with their fronts facing left. During the first car descent, wrist contact with a box flap stops the arm with an 8.2​cm8.2\,\mathrm{cm} vertical residual (tracking_error) and shifts the box across the table. Rather than repeatedly targeting coordinates measured before contact, the model treats the displaced container as state that must be restored: it sets down the held car, repositions the box to the central workspace, and revises subsequent trajectories to keep the wrists above the flaps with vertical descents and withdrawals.

In RoboCasa365 TurnOffStove (Fig. 15(b)), two distinct assumptions are contradicted in sequence during knob manipulation. First, after a secure grip turns the front-right knob only a few degrees before the execution receipt reports that rotation was stopped by mechanical resistance, the model keeps the verified knob target and releases only to reposition its wrist posture for a wider rotational range. Second, after the next turn brings the knob handle aligned horizontally along the stove—a pose that visually resembles the off position—the burner flame remains visibly blue in the camera view and the burner-on predicate stays true; recognizing that a symmetric handle alignment can occur halfway through a rotation, the model commands a further turn guided by the burner state until the flame extinguishes. Furthermore, when late corrections face a tight step limit—as in a swap_T episode where a 94∘94^{\circ} stem misalignment is detected at native step 345 with only 55 steps remaining (Tab. 21 in App. F)—paused-world preview rejects an initial 95-step correction and a 57-step revision before moving the robot, enabling the model to compress approach, rotation, release, and withdrawal into a 51-step coordinated trajectory that succeeds at step 396 (further replanning episodes on plug_in_charger, DeliverStraw, and SetUpCuttingStation are detailed in App. G).

Geometry-guided manipulation with VGGT-Omega and SAM 3.1. Fig. 16 compares recorded episodes with and without 3D geometric perception (Sec. 5.1) on matched scenes in RoboDojo and RoboCasa365.

On a randomized RoboDojo pack_objects_into_box scene (Fig. 16(a)), the VGGT-Omega/SAM 3.1 object table reports an initial 18∘18^{\circ} box yaw misalignment, prompting the model to grasp the front wall and rotate the box from 109∘109^{\circ} to 90∘90^{\circ} before packing; to grasp the hammer, querying pixel (267,274)(267,274) via geometry_query with a VGGT-derived center-height plane yields 𝐩query≃(−0.1051,−0.1827,0.7795)​m\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{query}}\simeq(-0.1051,-0.1827,0.7795)\,\mathrm{m}, guiding a finger-referenced grasp at (−0.105,−0.183,0.778)​m(-0.105,-0.183,0.778)\,\mathrm{m} to pack all four objects, whereas the run without VGGT/SAM exhausts the step limit.

On RoboCasa365 StackBowlsCabinet (Fig. 16(b)), the SAM 3.1 object table locates the open cabinet shelf top at 1.422​m1.422\,\mathrm{m}, the large-bowl rim at 0.991​m0.991\,\mathrm{m} (x=5.431​mx=5.431\,\mathrm{m}), and the small-bowl rim at 0.967​m0.967\,\mathrm{m} (x=5.502​mx=5.502\,\mathrm{m}); the model grasps each bowl 2​cm2\,\mathrm{cm} below its measured rim (0.968​m0.968\,\mathrm{m} and 0.948​m0.948\,\mathrm{m}) and places them at 1.477​m1.477\,\mathrm{m} inside the cabinet to succeed in 29 responses, whereas without the object table the large bowl slips at the cabinet opening, settles inverted on the counter, and eventually falls to the floor.

Failure modes under multi-body coupling and expanding recovery scope.

Fig. 17 illustrates two representative failure episodes where local corrections perturb coupled structures and exhaust the episode budget (step-by-step budget accounting in Tabs. 22 and 23 in App. G). In RoboDojo stack_bowls (Fig. 17(a)), after the model recovers from an initial slip to form a two-bowl stack (242 steps used, 558 left), placing the third bowl leaves it tilted; attempting to level the top bowl at step 440 lifts the nested three-bowl stack together, which slips and rolls onto its side during rotation, and subsequent supported pushes roll again upon arm withdrawal until the 800-step native budget expires (Score 15/100).

In RoboCasa365 HeatKebabSandwich (Fig. 17(b)), while loading a baguette into a toaster oven, contact with the oven entrance causes the bread to slip and land inside the oven below the wire rack at request 41, leaving its rack-contact predicate false. To expose the bread underneath, the model must pull out the wire rack—expanding the problem to grasping a thin front rail that repeatedly slips between requests 63 and 86; although the kebab is placed on the rack at request 50 and the rack finally slides outward at request 86, only 14 requests remain and the 100-request budget expires before the baguette can be lifted onto the rack. These failures highlight the boundary of kinematic trajectory execution: while stage verification and belief updates reliably detect discrepancies, recovery actions that disturb coupled multi-body assemblies or introduce secondary fixture obstacles can consume the remaining budget without achieving stable support.

7 Related Work

7.1 LLMs and VLMs for Embodied Reasoning

Robotic applications of language and vision-language models span task planning, spatial grounding, and direct action generation. Alongside general-purpose models such as GPT-6 [34] and Claude Opus 5.5 [1], embodied foundation models specialize perception and reasoning for physical interaction [12, 19, 45, 58, 6]. Evaluations of GPT-6 Astra [60, 10] investigate direct numerical control and cooperation with learned policies, revealing a gap between semantic task understanding and precise physical execution. Other work adapts robot behavior through context: GPT-Policy [5] preserves task-relevant demonstration transitions, while RoboICL [24] organizes demonstrations and interaction memory around observations, actions, and execution receipts.

7.2 Agentic Harnesses for Robotics

Agentic harnesses organize model interaction with robot tools, programs, and execution feedback. Trial-and-error interaction operates within a task: Agent as Policy [16] and CaP-Agent0 [9] within CaP-X allow agents to construct programs and revise execution using observations and tool results, while RoboHarness [38] emphasizes a visual-geometric control interface. The agent may also delegate action generation: PhysicalRSI [31] provides task-aware memory and skills backed by code policies or π0.5\pi_{0.5} [37], and FastHarness [22] adapts the frequency of VLM supervision over a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) model.

Cross-trial evolution uses rollout feedback to revise programs, tools, or policies for subsequent executions. HarnessPAI [48] keeps the generated program fixed within a rollout, including its observation-dependent checks, and revises it across rollouts. HexaShell [11] separates an acting agent from an optimizer that repairs and tests executable tools; EmbodiedEvo [20] separates exploration from evaluation, passing distilled code skills and failure lessons to independent test agents. Both freeze the acquired experience for evaluation without updating model weights. Related approaches evolve skills and context code, attribute execution failures, or select informative physical trials [47, 7, 44]; rollout scale and candidate selection also affect harness improvement [51]. WorldScape-R2SI [29] jointly improves reusable skills and a reactive action model, while ENPIRE [53] lets agents revise policy-training algorithms and infrastructure using real-robot evaluations.

Skill libraries complement cross-trial improvement by storing reusable procedures for later retrieval and composition. ASPIRE [26] stores validated repair knowledge as reusable in-context guidance, including applicability conditions, repair strategies, and optional code sketches; RATs [59] stores code skills acquired through self-directed play and retrieves them from a frozen library for downstream tasks. Teach-and-Grow [33] derives closed-loop Skill Blocks from subgoals shared across demonstrations and retains execution conditions and repairs in a separate experience memory. Real2Gym [39] retains task procedures, object-relative motions, and recovery strategies from interaction in simulation environments reconstructed from videos, then reuses them on physical robots. GaP [3] focuses on composition, assembling existing perception, planning, and control modules into computation graphs refined through simulation. Auriga organizes interaction within a persistent model session, where generated programs and direct tool calls share a physical execution interface and return observations and outcomes to guide subsequent decisions.

7.3 Vision-Language-Action and World Action Models

Learned action models map visual and language inputs to robot actions and can serve as policies invoked by an agent. Recent VLA work explores heterogeneous-data co-training and cross-embodiment adaptation [37, 62, 35, 52, 54, 56], experience-driven policy improvement [36], and joint reasoning and action generation [25]. InternVLA-A1.5 [28] further introduces latent foresight supervised by a pretrained video model while retaining semantic training objectives.

World action models (WAMs) incorporate predictive modeling or supervision from future observations into action learning.
