Video-based approaches jointly model actions and future observations [55, 18, 50]; VPP2 [14] strengthens manipulation-specific video prediction, and X-WAM [13] adds multi-view RGB-D prediction with asynchronous action decoding. Future supervision can also shape action representations without requiring future-video generation at deployment, as in Being-H0.7, Fast-WAM, and InternW0-Δ\Delta [27, 57, 30]. JEPA-WAM [23] couples latent transition prediction to action generation, while Long-WAM [15] studies causal pretraining and longer observation histories. When these policies are used within a harness, the agent coordinates their invocation, evaluates execution outcomes, and revises the task procedure.

8 Conclusion

We have presented Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness for zero-shot manipulation within a single episode, closing 68.3% of the planning–execution gap of vision-language models on RoboDojo (from 22.5% under the reference interface toward the 76.2% arm-free upper bound) without target-task exploration, demonstrations, or environment resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief BtB_{t} and acts through direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D perception, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway 𝒜\mathcal{A} that previews trajectories while simulation is paused and verifies stage tolerances and grasp bounds during execution for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first overall on the 42-task RoboDojo leaderboard with a 64.0 Score and 57.7% success rate, maintains first place under scene randomization (G=46.3G=46.3) while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%, and achieves a 73.2% success rate on RoboCasa365 mobile manipulation. Future work will extend this closed-loop execution architecture toward continuous force-sensitive manipulation, lower deliberation latency, and automated cross-task tool synthesis.

Appendix A Benchmark Tasks and Evaluation Scope

Tab. 13 lists the 42 tasks of RoboDojo by capability dimension (Sec. 6.1.1).

Evaluation protocol comparison scope (Tab. 1).

Tab. 1 in Sec. 2.1 distinguishes target-task environment trials from offline demonstration analysis. Prepared code/skills include procedures later generalized across tasks; trial-derived memory denotes separate notes inherited from earlier trials. Demo-derived artifacts are distilled text or code, whereas demo references are recorded images or motions, including those retrieved from frozen packages. Task-independent tools, public task specifications, current-episode history, benchmark-required memory events, and training data encoded in model weights are outside these categories. A fixed evaluation agent does not establish the absence of earlier task-driven tool development: PyRUA-Lean uses shared primitives without cross-episode memory, but does not report whether target-task trials informed their development, so its two preparation entries are marked as not reported [43]; HexaShell is shown for non-Open tasks, as its Open setting omits task-specific development and notes [11]; and the R2SI row describes the inspected public release, where outer-loop trials exclude Open tasks and the snapshot supplies no separate memory files or demo context, although the framework supports memory updates and its WAMs use trained weights [29].

Appendix F Extended Execution Trace Analysis

We examine swap_T, a pose-exchange task in the Memory dimension, to study how a remembered objective guides manipulation after the scene changes (complementing the matched-scene baseline comparison in Secs. 6.5 and 12). The robot must exchange two T-shaped blocks so that each occupies the other’s initial position and orientation. This task combines three demands in a compact setting: preserving a spatial reference after its source object moves, coordinating access to a shared workspace, and correcting the object pose when grasping or release changes it. The asymmetric T shape makes orientation part of the goal, so exchanging positions alone is insufficient. We analyze the 15-scene standard-variant diagnostic set for this task, using their task-belief records, action specifications, execution receipts, and evaluator outcomes.

Preserving object goals across changes in execution.

For analysis, let T^A,0\hat{T}_{A,0} and T^B,0\hat{T}_{B,0} denote the two initial planar poses comprising planar position and yaw estimated from the calibrated images. The exchange assigns the object goals

GA=T^B,0,GB=T^A,0.G_{A}=\hat{T}_{B,0},\qquad G_{B}=\hat{T}_{A,0}. (5)

These goals remain fixed when the model changes a grasp or assigns the remaining transfer to another arm. The current object location and its relation to the gripper, however, must be updated from subsequent observations. This distinction matters after slippage: re-localizing the fallen block supplies a new pickup pose, while the saved initial pose still supplies its destination. The recorded task_plan separates these roles through the plan, attention, and ledger described in Sec. 3.3. Its updates retain the original placement requirement while revising which physical conditions are supported and which remain unresolved.

A completed motion can still require a task-level correction. Tab. 19 follows a successful exchange in which the pink block has already reached the blue block’s initial pose. During the remaining right-arm transfer, the blue block slips onto the table. The crossing stage reports completed, but its grip feedback records a zero final aperture, and the returned image places the block to the left of its target. The next belief revision marks blue retention as contradicted while retaining the pink placement as supported. The model then selects the nearby left arm, re-localizes the blue stem, and specifies a short, slow transfer to the original target. Thus the correction changes the arm, pickup coordinates, and transport motion together, while preserving both the completed placement and the outstanding object goal.

Recovery preserves completed work. The two ledger entries distinguish an unresolved blue transfer from an already supported pink placement. Consequently, the model does not repeat the entire exchange or derive a new destination from the displaced scene. It repairs the remaining relation between one object and its saved goal. This is the operational value of maintaining task state: evidence can invalidate a local assumption without erasing the broader objective or the progress already achieved. It also explains why counting only tracking_error receipts would miss an important class of recovery. Here, the discrepancy lies between successful robot motion and unsuccessful object transport, and is exposed by combining the receipt with the resulting observation.

Using feedback to revise feasible operations.

Tab. 20 summarizes mechanism use across the 15 episodes. Geometric queries provide coordinates for pickup and placement; belief updates retain the goal and revise progress; previews evaluate candidate operations before execution. All episodes use each of these capabilities. Their roles become concrete in the preceding trace: the saved target survives the transfer failure, a fresh localization supplies the new grasp, and the revised action specification changes which arm performs the remaining work. The table counts usage at the interface where it occurs, including calls made through model-written programs.

Coordination is expressed at the scale of an operation. Multi-stage plans account for 73 of the 74 generated plans. The sequence can include pickup, lift, transfer, release, and withdrawal, allowing the model to consider the entire operation before committing to it. The 54 plans involving both arms include staggered motion and one-arm holding while the other places an object. This is well suited to pose exchange: both destinations are initially occupied, and the arms need access to the same central region. The recorded plans repeatedly resolve this dependency by holding one block clear, delivering the other, and then completing the exchange. The relevant coordination is the ordering of access and the preservation of held objects, which can be expressed within one plan even when the arms move at different times.

Preview makes correction cost available before motion. A second successful exchange shows how the model uses the remaining budget when a late observation contradicts placement. After 345 native steps, the blue block is correctly placed, but the red block’s stem points in the wrong direction. The next belief revision preserves the required destination and calls for a right-arm re-grasp and approximately 94-degree clockwise correction. Tab. 21 records the subsequent candidate costs. With 55 steps remaining, the model shortens the route and coordinates gripper motion with the approach and return. The executed specification also contains an explicit release stage. Task success is reached at step 396. The useful change is therefore more specific than issuing another grasp: the correction is reorganized to include the outstanding orientation change, release, and return within the available budget.

The 106 preview evaluations and 74 generated plans in Tab. 20 reflect this distinction between evaluating a candidate and obtaining a plan for execution. The remaining 32 evaluations report unsuccessful candidates without generating such a plan. Likewise, the observation pause provides an opportunity to inspect intermediate results; it is counted separately from grasp-guard specifications and execution errors. The two traces show how deliberation and physical execution interact: one revises the physical route after object loss, while the other revises the cost and timing of a correction before moving. Together with the matched-scene comparison against RoboProbe in Tab. 12 (Sec. 6.5), these records connect task-level objectives to concrete physical operations.

Appendix G Extended Case Studies

This appendix provides the extended RoboDojo and RoboCasa365 case analyses accompanying Sec. 6.6: additional recovery episodes after slippage (Figs. 22 and 23), replanning episodes after contact and execution disruptions (Figs. 24 and 25), and detailed step-by-step budget accounting for the failure episodes (Tabs. 22 and 23).

Additional slippage recovery episodes.

Alongside sequence reproduction and lettuce washing (Fig. 14 in Sec. 6.6), Figs. 22 and 23 show how the model separates acquisition, retention during transport, and post-release support on conveyor picking, bowl stacking, and drawer-to-counter transfer.

Conveyor picking: separating acquisition, retention, and destination access. The model must match a figurine to the board image, place it inside the basket, and lift the basket by more than 8 cm. The moving conveyor first invalidates a basket pickup location, prompting a switch to right-arm interception. For the figurine, an approach contacts the hat before closure; a later empty closure leaves the body exposed. A torso grasp then acquires the object, but the figurine slips during transport (Fig. 22(a)). The model consequently changes both the grasp and the transfer conditions: it moves the basket aside, re-grasps across the torso, and verifies retention during a slower lift.

Once the figurine is retained, the remaining obstacle is the destination. Moving the basket underneath it causes contact with the image board and tilts the opening. The model keeps the figurine held, moves the basket upward and away from the board, and then completes the release. A later check against the initial image revises the height judgment because the earlier estimate followed a rim on a tilted basket. The loaded basket is raised farther before the evaluator signals success. These successive revisions address distinct predicates (target acquired, target retained, opening accessible, and required basket elevation), so progress on one predicate can be preserved while another is corrected.

Bowl stacking: changing the assembly order after a failed lift. The initial plan uses the rear middle bowl as the base, adds the left bowl, and then adds the right bowl. The first rim grip slips and displaces the left bowl. The revised plan lets that bowl settle while the robot approaches the right bowl, using a deeper pinch and slower lift (Fig. 22(b)). After the right bowl is nested into the base and remains supported after release, the model re-localizes the displaced left bowl and adds it last. Thus recovery changes the assembly order as well as the grasp.

This reordering is possible because the task constrains the final stack rather than the order in which bowls enter it. It also gives the displaced bowl time to settle before its next localization. The plan checks co-motion after lifting and upright support after release and withdrawal; the final return supplies another observation of whether the stack persists without gripper support. The evaluator confirms successful stacking. The distinction from sequence reproduction is consequential: the bowl order can change to simplify execution, whereas the observed object order must remain fixed.

Drawer-to-counter transfer: shifting contact from a thin handle to the wider bowl. The robot must take a ladle from an open drawer and place it on the counter, where the single task predicate tests only whether the ladle rests on the counter and remains false until final placement. An initial grasp on the thin handle slips during the lift, and after a lower re-grasp on a thicker section of the handle, the ladle slips again during mobile-base motion and falls back into the drawer (Fig. 23). Both losses are reported by the execution receipts rather than the task predicate, and after the second slip the object table no longer finds the ladle in the wrist-camera view.

The model revises its task plan to grasp the ladle’s wider bowl instead, though roughly ten attempts are blocked by the counter overhang or miss inside the drawer while it pulls the drawer out farther. It then uses the handle to draw the ladle forward within the drawer and grasps the bowl once clear of the overhang. Transferring the ladle by its bowl and releasing it on the counter turns the placement predicate true, and the evaluator confirms task success. This revision corresponds to the acquisition condition at the start of Sec. 6.6: when a thin handle fails to sustain lift and base transport, recovery changes the contact geometry to a wider region of the object.

Additional contact and replanning episodes.

Alongside object packing and burner shutoff (Fig. 15 in Sec. 6.6), Figs. 24 and 25 follow the model from a measured discrepancy to a procedure revision across conveyor picking, charger insertion, straw delivery, and cutting-station setup.

Conveyor picking: using support to decouple placement from basket motion. The cup initially remains held while the other arm raises the basket. During approach, the basket swings and the cup shifts in the left grip; a wrist-orientation change then loses the cup. After recovering it with a body grasp, the model preserves that wrist orientation and changes the basket procedure (Fig. 24(a)). The revised plan lowers the basket onto the belt, loads the cup, and then lifts the filled basket above the required height.

Supporting the basket changes the manipulation problem. Insertion can now be organized around a supported opening, while lifting becomes a separate operation on the loaded container. When a side adjustment loses the handle grip, the plan retains the cup grasp, clears the right arm for placement, and postpones handle acquisition until the cup has been released. The model then verifies that the cup stays inside after left-arm withdrawal, re-grasps the handle from above, and lifts the basket to complete the task. This sequence preserves the final object-in-basket and elevation requirements while removing the need to maintain a suspended basket throughout insertion.

Charger insertion: revising only the part of the procedure contradicted by evidence. The initial plan allows a table-supported handover if the left arm cannot reach the socket. A preview establishes a direct route, so the model keeps the charger in the left hand and moves the right arm outward to clear that route. Near the socket, the clear_pins clearance lift returns tracking_error: the position error is 3.27 mm, predominantly vertical, exceeding the stage’s tight 3 mm tolerance. The charger remains held, and camera measurements identify a small lateral alignment correction (Fig. 24(b)). The next action uses the returned position to center the pins and complete the insertion, followed by release and a check that the charger stays seated.

The later return-path failure calls for a different revision. Because seating remains visually supported, the model leaves the inserted charger undisturbed and splits the right-arm return into shorter movements through clear intermediate poses. The evaluator then reports success. This separates a local alignment correction from a route-planning problem: one changes the target relative to the socket, while the other changes how the arm reaches its home pose. Neither requires repeating the already verified insertion.

Straw delivery: matching the scope of revision to the invalidated assumption. The task requires taking a straw from a drawer to a glass cup on the dining counter; initially, the object table locates the drawer handles while neither the straw nor the cup is visible. Repeated attempts to open the first drawer return execution receipts for a blocked or stalled approach (Fig. 25(a)), as approaching the handle from above brings the gripper against the counter. The model switches to a horizontal approach from the robot-facing side of the handle, backs the mobile base away for clearance, and writes that direction into the grasp stage before pulling the drawer open with the base.

Inspecting the opened drawer reveals a different discrepancy when the object table finds no straw inside. The task plan records that this drawer is empty while the adjacent front drawer remains unchecked, and the robot opens that second drawer using the same horizontal handle approach and base pull. After grasping the straw and driving around the counter end, it rights the glass after a missed first insertion, places the straw inside to satisfy the straw-in-cup predicate, and backs away as the evaluator confirms success. As in charger insertion, the two disruptions call for different scopes of revision: a blocked grasp changes the approach route, whereas an empty drawer changes the target container without altering the delivery objective.

Cutting-station setup: restoring a displaced container before revising the approach. The task requires taking a knife from a drawer and a fish from a plate and placing both onto a cutting board. When the arm reaches downward for the knife, the execution receipt reports a blocked approach, and the camera view shows that arm contact has pushed the partly open drawer inward (Fig. 25(b)). The model initially plans to raise the arm, reopen the drawer, and approach from above with more clearance.

Across roughly ten subsequent attempts, however, passing the arm over the drawer front repeatedly pushes the drawer inward and leaves grasps blocked or empty. The model then pulls the drawer fully open, withdraws the gripper clear of the handle before turning the wrist to approach from the side, and lowers its grasp slightly to place the finger pads around the knife handle. Delivering the knife satisfies the knife-on-board predicate, and after the fish is re-grasped following a slip during base motion, the evaluator signals task success during the final placement onto the board. As in object packing, the central revision treats the displaced drawer as state that must be restored and paired with a non-colliding approach route, rather than targeting coordinates measured before contact.

Detailed budget accounting for failure episodes.

Tabs. 22 and 23 give the step-by-step native motion and model-request budget accounting for the failed stack_bowls and HeatKebabSandwich episodes shown in Fig. 17 (Sec. 6.6).

Steps used Steps left State guiding the next decision
242 558 Two bowls remain nested after withdrawal; add the third.
440 360 The third bowl remains tilted after seating attempts; re-grasp and level it.
564 236 The nested stack was lifted and slipped; restore it using table support.
691 109 The stack has rolled onto its side again during the return; attempt a compact supported correction.
756 44 The rim pinch has not retained the stack; change contact to the raised base.
800 0 Native step limit reached; task failure, Score 15/100.
Requests used Requests left State guiding the next decision
14 86 The baguette has slipped onto the counter beside the open door; re-grasp it with an explicit approach direction.
41 59 The baguette is inside the oven but below the wire rack, so its rack-contact check is false; move the rack to expose the bread.
51 49 The kebab rests on the rack and its check passes; slide the loaded rack inward and recover the baguette from below.
63 37 The rack has not moved because the grip on its thin front rail was not secure; grasp the rail from a raised angle.
86 14 The rack has slid outward with the kebab, leaving the baguette behind it; lift the bread onto the rack.
97 3 The model reports the task unfinished: kebab on the rack, baguette below it, door open; the harness asks it to continue.
100 0 Model-request limit reached; task failure.

Coupled structures and local completion versus cumulative progress. In stack_bowls (Tab. 22), the plan at step 440 intends to lift and level the tilted top bowl, but the grasp lifts the entire nested stack, changing the recovery target from seating one bowl to restoring upright support for all three bowls. Although subsequent tipping maneuvers, supported pushes, and contact changes receive completed motion receipts, the structure rolls again upon arm withdrawal as the remaining budget drops from 360 steps to 44. Similarly, in HeatKebabSandwich (Tab. 23), after the baguette lands below the toaster wire rack at request 41, exposing the bread requires pulling the thin front rail of the rack, which repeatedly slips between requests 63 and 86; although placing the kebab at request 50 and sliding the rack outward at request 86 succeed locally, only 14 requests remain and the 100-request budget expires before the baguette is lifted onto the rack.
